While in Duval County, I was pleased to announce $26.5 million in projected federal transportation funding that will help move critical projects forward.

More than 80 percent of the transportation funding programmed for the county under this plan is supported by federal dollars. These funds will improve roads and bridges along SH 359, SH 44, US 59 and FM 2295, including the rehabilitation of approximately 10 miles of FM 2295 and bridge improvements along SH 359.

These projects will help make roads safer, improve connections to jobs, schools and health care, and support the families, businesses and communities that rely on this infrastructure every day.

I’ll continue working to bring federal transportation dollars back to South Texas and ensure rural communities like those in Duval County have the infrastructure they need to keep moving forward.

text:
Last Wednesday, I visited a Habitat for Humanity site build in Macon, GA. Over the past year and a half, the cost of living has skyrocketed. It is not just more expensive to put food on the table or fill the gas tank, it is also harder to buy or rent a home. Gutting the workers at USDA that help our farmers as well as chaotic tariffs and an unauthorized war in Iran have driving up the cost of fuel, disrupted crucial supply chains for everything from the food we eat to the materials we use to build housing.

While I continue to work hard in Congress to rein that in, I was glad to work with Democrats and Republicans this summer to pass the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act which will help improve the housing supply and prevent large corporations from scooping up chunks of property that make it harder for hardworking Americans to afford a home.

I continue working with municipal and county governments as well as community organizations to direct federal funds to local projects that help develop housing right here in Middle and Southwest Georgia so that it is a more affordable place to live, work, and raise a family.

I helped secure more than $1 billion in the FY26 Transportation, Housing, and Urban Development Appropriations bill for HUD’s Housing for the Elderly program, a nearly $100 million increase over FY24.

For seniors in South Texas living on fixed incomes, rising housing costs can make it harder to find a safe and affordable place to call home. I will continue working through the appropriations process to support affordable housing and make sure South Texas seniors have safe and accessible housing.

text:
The Trump administration's rollback of fuel economy standards actually will cost you more in the long run. 

Its own analysis shows why.

It projects Americans will spend about $1,600 more on gasoline over the life of each new vehicle (that estimate assumes gas at $3.30/gallon).

The administration says the rollback will cut the price of manufacturing a new car by $1,300. 

But nothing requires automakers to pass those savings along to consumers. 

If automakers keep the savings, drivers get the higher fuel bills and nothing to offset them. So what is this really all about? 

More profits for oil companies. 

About 122 billion more gallons of fuel will be used through 2050. Meaning more air pollution for all of us.

I want cars to be more affordable and I want families to keep more of what they earn. Efficient vehicles are how you get both, and they shield drivers from price swings at the pump.
https://t.co/7ekBVmxaVY

In addition to being plainly negligent, these children are being denied due process under the Constitution of the United States of America. I have been a voice on this issue for as long as I have served in Congress, but recent events have shown unprecedented levels of cruelty by this administration that must stop once and for all.

The allegations of sexual assault at Cornell University are deeply horrifying. I commend this young woman for her courage in seeking justice, and I fully support the district attorney’s decision to reopen the criminal investigation. 

But the victims of heinous crimes should not be forced to fight an uphill battle for justice while they work to heal from the trauma inflicted upon them. This case, and far too many like it, are the product of a culture of violence against women and systems that silence survivors at college campuses across our country. 

There must be a full and independent investigation into the alleged crimes and the role of the authorities who managed this case from the very beginning. Moreover, each and every one of us has a role in preventing violence against women by confronting wrongdoing and standing with survivors.

This should be on the front page of every newspaper in America. 

Trump cut a deal with one of the most corrupt and violent gold mining companies in Venezuela, a company that the U.S. has designated a threat to our national security and one whose miners pay protection money to a local gang. 

The U.S. has imposed sanctions on Venezuelan gold for years and for good reason: the industry has been tied to gangs, corrupt military officials, human-rights abuses, and illicit financing. 

So why is the Trump Administration importing hundreds of millions of dollars of it?

After intervening in Venezuela, the Trump Administration tried to turn Venezuelan gold into a quick economic and geopolitical win. Except they didn’t do their homework. 

They didn’t confirm that the gold was clean. Now we know some of the gold is connected to local gangs.

text: Today marks 50 years of harm, hardship, and uncertainty under the Hyde Amendment. Since its adoption in 1976, the Hyde Amendment has relentlessly and brutally restricted a woman's right to make her own healthcare decisions. Its vile legacy can be seen in the countless women it has affected over this painful past century, as well as in every regression in this nation that its very existence has made possible. Indeed, the Supreme Court’s decision to overturn Roe v. Wade and deny millions of women their right to an abortion could only have arrived in the wake of a post-Hyde America, where women’s autonomy has remained under siege, and our personal medical decisions are offered to all hands but our own.

text: While there is no shortage of cruelties lurking in the laws of this nation, the Hyde Amendment is particularly sickening because its negative impacts are felt mostly by those with the least. For half a century, it has blocked low-income Americans from having access to insurance when seeking abortion coverage. For Black and brown women, as well as those belonging to rural communities who have long navigated systemic discrimination and contended with trauma and hardship in their struggle to receive care, its impact and consequences have been especially devastating.

text: Systemic injustice does not occur spontaneously. It is born in the cruel and controlling hearts of politicians who steal our power and pretend it is their own. As Members of Congress, we have a moral responsibility to stop the Hyde Amendment before it reaches one more year and harms any more women. Now is the time we come together to put an end to this vicious chapter in our history. That starts with passing the EACH Act and ensuring that every American can access affordable abortion care, no matter what.
